title: Let's All Go to the World's Fair
summary: Josh and Chuck (Jerry is away) trace the history of world's fairs, also called international or universal expositions. They start with 1700s English industrial arts shows and France's early exhibitions, then cover the 1851 Great Exhibition (Crystal Palace) in London, the 1853 New York exhibition, Philadelphia's 1876 Centennial, Paris expositions (including 1889 with the Eiffel Tower and Hygiene Palace, and 1900 with the Cinerama), Latin American and colonial-era fairs, the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition (Ferris wheel, zipper, Westinghouse lighting, brief mention of H.H. Holmes), the 1904 St. Louis fair (cotton candy, hot dog buns, ice cream cones, electric plug), the Bureau International des Expositions rules from 1928/1931, the 1939 and 1964 New York fairs, Seattle's 1962 Century 21 Expo, the 1984 New Orleans fair and its financial failure, Osaka 1970, and Shanghai 2010, plus upcoming fairs. The episode ends with listener mail about the MacGuffin.

entities.name: Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations

segments.title: Opening banter and framing
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on world's fairs, noting Jerry is away, and frame fairs as a way people once saw new technology and ideas.

segments.title: Early exhibitions in England and France
segments.summary: Early industrial arts shows in England in the 1700s, the Society for Arts, and France starting its own shows in the late 1700s as a national competition and showcase.

segments.title: The 1851 Great Exhibition and Crystal Palace
segments.summary: Prince Albert hosted the 1851 Great Exhibition in Hyde Park, housed in Joseph Paxton's glass and iron Crystal Palace, with about 14,000 exhibits, and it made money. Other early fairs followed in Dublin, Cork, Munich and New York; New York's 1853 show was less successful.

segments.title: Paris rises and the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial
segments.summary: Paris took over as the center of fairs. The US's first successful fair was the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial, where the typewriter was invented and Bell demonstrated the telephone, and the Corliss steam engine powered the machines.

segments.title: Paris expositions and fountains
segments.summary: Paris hosted eight fairs between 1855 and 1937, often showing off political achievements. The 1889 Fountain of Progress had electric lights shining up from underwater.

segments.title: The 1889 Paris Expo: Eiffel Tower and Hygiene Palace
segments.summary: The 1889 Exposition Universelle debuted the Eiffel Tower, which Parisians nearly saw torn down until it was used as a radio telegraph station. The Hygiene Palace showed medical and childcare exhibits, including a replica of the tower at a foundling hospital.

segments.title: The 1900 Paris Expo: Cinerama and the Black American exhibit
segments.summary: The 1900 Paris exposition drew about fifty million people and debuted a Cinerama simulated balloon ride. An exhibit by American Black scholars, including W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington, showed progress since slavery through photographs and infographics.
topics: W. E. B. Du Bois infographics

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break for iHeartRadio sponsor reads.

segments.title: Latin American and colonial world's fairs
segments.summary: Latin American countries after independence held their own fairs in the 1870s and 1880s, including Cordoba, Buenos Aires and Santiago. Tensions existed between showing industry and showing raw materials for exploitation. Colonial fairs were held in Calcutta, Kingston, and Hanoi.

segments.title: Chicago 1893 World's Columbian Exposition
segments.summary: The Chicago fair is introduced as the most famous US fair of its era, with notes on the H. H. Holmes serial killer story, the Devil in the White City book, and inventions like Cracker Jacks, the dishwasher, and the zipper.

segments.title: Ferris wheel origins and off-topic chatter
segments.summary: The first Ferris wheel was built for the 1893 fair, 264 feet tall with 36 cars, and cost fifty cents for a ride. Hosts discuss modern Ferris wheels in Atlanta and London, followed by off-topic talk about a Simpsons joke and a movie.

segments.title: Electrical lighting and Chicago architecture
segments.summary: Westinghouse won the contract over Edison to light the 1893 fair. The fair's white neoclassical buildings, the White City, influenced American architecture. Art deco came from the 1925 Paris exhibit, and Napier, New Zealand was rebuilt in art deco after a 1931 earthquake.

segments.title: St. Louis 1904 fair and junk food firsts
segments.summary: The 1904 St. Louis fair is discussed, along with the musical Meet Me in St. Louis, and claims it introduced hamburgers, hot dogs, and ice cream cones. Hot dogs were first served in buns there, cotton candy was introduced as fairy floss by dentist William J. Morrison, Dr Pepper and Jell-O debuted, and the first electric plug and socket appeared. The fair also included offensive human exhibits about Indigenous and colonized peoples.

segments.title: Break before the next section
segments.summary: A short break before the second half of the episode.

segments.title: Bureau International des Expositions and rules
segments.summary: After World War One, fairs declined as radio and movies spread and too many fairs competed. The Bureau International des Expositions established rules in 1928, with official sanctioning starting in 1931, including government approval, time limits and themes.

segments.title: Cold War fairs and the 1939 New York World's Fair
segments.summary: Cold War fairs became stages for US-Soviet competition. The 1939 New York World of Tomorrow fair debuted air conditioning, television and nylon stockings, featured the robot Electro, and reclaimed Flushing Meadows. Germany was barred from its pavilion after invading Czechoslovakia.

segments.title: The 1964 New York World's Fair and Asimov's essay
segments.summary: The 1964 New York fair debuted Disney's It's a Small World, GE's Carousel of Progress, and an Illinois animatronic Lincoln. Isaac Asimov wrote an essay predicting the 2014 fair, getting robots and enforced leisure partly right.

segments.title: Seattle 1962 and the decline of US fairs; New Orleans 1984
segments.summary: The 1962 Seattle Century 21 Expo gave us the Space Needle; attendance declined after. The 1984 Louisiana World Exposition in New Orleans was heavy on local culture, had unfinished parts, and drew under ten million visitors, with a financial loss.

segments.title: Knoxville 1982 and the later fair era
segments.summary: The 1982 Knoxville World's Fair, the 1984 Olympics, and the oil bust hurt New Orleans and regional attendance. The Nineteen Ninety Two Chicago fair was canceled after the New Orleans losses. The center of fairs moved toward Asia and the Middle East.

segments.title: Osaka 1970, Shanghai 2010 and upcoming expos
segments.summary: Osaka 1970 introduced IMAX films. Shanghai 2010 is cited as the most-attended fair with about 73 million visitors. Upcoming fairs include Osaka 2025, Belgrade 2027, and Riyadh 2030. Chuck notes his parents met at Expo 70.

segments.title: Listener mail about the MacGuffin
segments.summary: Listeners respond to a short stuff episode on the MacGuffin. A writer-director explains the device as a plot placeholder. Hosts discuss whether the Maltese Falcon and R2-D2 are MacGuffins, and Chuck shares a story about seeing Charlie Sheen's co-star at a McDonald's.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck sign off and the show credits iHeartRadio.
